To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the population dynamics of the rhizobia in nodules and the rhizosphere are different and that this is due to the diversifying and frequency-dependent selection of different rhizobia by their hosts.
the population structures of Rhizobia in the nodules of different host plants are shaped by diversifying selection and frequency-dependent selection.

the population structures of Rhizobia in the rhizosphere and in nodules are different and that the “rhizosphere to nodule” transition may be diversifying for the whole population and frequency dependent for individual OTUs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the population dynamics and evolution of rhizobial populations in the rhizosphere and nodules of leguminous plants.
the population dynamics of rhizobial species in the rhizospheres of leguminous plants and the mechanisms of selection of rhizobium variants in the nodules of different host plants.
the population dynamics of rhizobia in nodules of different hosts, which are the main factor in determining the evolutionary fate of these symbionts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the natural selection in rhizobia is a complex process that depends on the population structure, phylogeny and symbiotic specificity of the interacting rhizobia and their host legumes.
the rhizosphere → nodule transition is not a simple selection process, but a complex one that is dependent upon the symbiotic specificity of the bacteria and the host species.

the natural selection in the populations of R. leguminosarrom is frequency-dependent and diversifying, and that the diversifying selection is responsible for the maintenance of the diversity of the symbiotic partners in the natural environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the natural selection of rhizobia is a complex process that involves both diversifying selection (which maintains the diversity of rhizobia) and frequency-dependent selection (which maintains specific interactions of rhizobia with their host plants).
the population structure and dynamics of rhizobia are influenced by the symbiotic specificity of the host plant.

the population dynamics of rhizobia is a consequence of the interaction of the following factors: 1) the specificity of the host plant, 2) the specificity of symbiotic genes, 3) the phylogenetic position of the rhizobia and 4) their ecological niches.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the population dynamics of nodule bacteria in the rhizospheric environment is driven by the selection pressure exerted by different host plants.
the population structures of the nodule bacteria are determined by the host species and the type of natural-selection processes that occur during the symbiotic interaction.
the population structure of rhizobia is determined by the type of natural and sexual selection and by the type of host plant.
